summary.text: Lesson 5 of Wordly Wise 3000 Book 9: fifteen words about judgement and character (sagacious, cynical, callow, indolent, voracious), power and hardship (despot, impoverish, impediment, strife), and time and belief (contemporary, secular, wane, speculate, venerate, enunciate).

why.text: Half this list is about how people judge each other — sagacious, cynical, callow, venerate. Which word a writer picks tells you whose side they are on, often more clearly than anything they argue.

objectives.text: Define and use all fifteen Lesson 5 words correctly
Use contemporary correctly as a noun, not only as “modern”
Distinguish degree, type-to-category and “lacks” relationships in analogies
Recognize when near-synonyms carry opposite sympathies

parentNote.text: Built from the Lesson 5 word list. Contemporary is the trap worth checking: as a noun it means someone living at the same time as another person, with no implication of being modern — two questions target that directly. One analogy (VENERATE : RESPECT) deliberately has no perfect answer and asks her to pick the closest structure after eliminating; that is a real standardized-test skill and the explanation says so plainly.

nextUp.text: Cards, then the quiz. Sagacious and voracious sound alike and mean nothing alike — check both.

cards.def:
**Young and inexperienced; immature.** (adjective)
• The student was too callow to know he was being fooled.
• It originally described an unfledged bird — no feathers yet.

**A person living during the same period as another.** (noun)
• Calamity Jane and Annie Oakley were contemporaries.
• As an adjective: existing at the same time — the fuel-cost rise was contemporary with the demand for alternatives.
cards.hint: It does NOT only mean modern. Two ancient Romans can be contemporaries.

cards.def:
**Doubtful of the sincerity of others’ motives; skeptical.** (adjective)
• People become cynical about those who make promises and do not keep them.
• cynic (n): the attorney has heard many lies and still has not become a cynic.

**A ruler with absolute power or tyrannical control.** (noun)
• Divided government makes rule by a despot less likely.
• despotic (adj): the Declaration of Independence asserts a right to overthrow a despotic ruler.

**To pronounce clearly.** (verb)
• In speech class we learn to enunciate our words.
• Second meaning: to state or announce — she enunciated her objectives for the coming year.

**Anything that gets in the way; an obstacle.** (noun)
• After the hurricane, fallen trees were impediments to traffic.
• Ped- means foot — an impediment is literally something your feet catch on.

**To make poor.** (verb)
• Uncontrolled spending can impoverish a person.
• Second meaning: to take away — continual overfarming impoverishes the soil.

**Indulging in ease; avoiding exertion; lazy.** (adjective)
• Being in the torrid heat of the tropical sun makes one feel indolent.
• indolence (n): his failure cannot be blamed on indolence.

**Showing sound judgement; wise.** (adjective)
• My grandmother’s sagacious advice has guided me for years.
• sagacity (n): she questioned the sagacity of my plan to climb the mountain.

**Worldly; not connected with a church or religion.** (adjective)
• The choir included a few secular songs in the memorial service.
• The near-twin of temporal from Lesson 4 — both mean “of this world”.

**To think about or make guesses.** (verb)
• As we waited, we speculated about whether he would show up.
• Second meaning: to engage in a risky business venture — she lost money speculating in stocks.

**Conflict or struggle.** (noun)
• The strife between the two families has gone on for years.
• Bigger and longer-running than an argument.

**To show great respect for.** (verb)
• Asian cultures venerate their ancestors long after they have died.
• Veneration is respect with reverence in it — stronger than admiration.

**Ravenous; desiring and eating a large amount of food.** (adjective)
• We came back from our hike with voracious appetites.
• Second meaning: greatly eager — Danyal has been a voracious reader since childhood.

**To get smaller, dimmer, or weaker; to near an end.** (verb)
• When interest in sitcoms waned, the networks switched to reality shows.
• The moon wanes after it is full — that is where the word lives most naturally.
cards.hint: Wane shrinks, wax grows. The moon does both.

questions.hint: It originally described a bird with no feathers yet.
steps: Callow means young and inexperienced; immature.
A student too callow to know he was being fooled lacks the experience to spot it.
Wisdom is close to its opposite.

ex.main: **Young and inexperienced.** The image behind it is an unfledged bird, not yet able to fly.
ex.tip: Callow is almost always slightly critical — it implies the inexperience is showing.

questions.hint: It is respect with reverence in it.
steps: Venerate means to show great respect for.
Venerating ancestors long after their deaths is respect approaching reverence.
The wrong options define cynical, impoverish and enunciate.

ex.main: **Show them great respect.** Veneration goes beyond admiration toward reverence.
ex.tip: Three of the four options are also Lesson 5 words. Ruling them out by definition is faster than weighing feel.

questions.q: What does it mean when interest in something wanes?
opts: It weakens and nears an end
questions.hint: Think of the moon after it is full.
steps: Wane means to get smaller, dimmer or weaker; to near an end.
Interest in sitcoms waning is why networks switched to reality shows.
Growing is wax, its opposite.

ex.main: **It weakens and nears an end.** Wane and wax are the pair — one shrinks, one grows.
ex.tip: Waxing and waning are worth memorising together; tests like opposites that travel as a set.

opts: An obstacle that gets in the way
steps: An impediment is anything that gets in the way.
Fallen trees after a hurricane were impediments to traffic.
The root ped- (foot) gives the picture: something your feet catch on.

ex.main: **An obstacle.** Impediment shares its root with pedestrian and pedal — all about feet.
ex.tip: Root-spotting is the cheapest vocabulary tool there is. Ped-, sed-, and tract- each unlock a dozen words.

questions.q: A despot is a ruler who:
opts: Is elected for a fixed term
questions.hint: Divided government makes this kind of rule less likely.
steps: A despot is a ruler with absolute power or tyrannical control over a group of people.
Divided government makes despotism less likely because power is shared.
Elections, councils and ceremonial roles all limit power — the opposite of despotism.

ex.main: **Absolute or tyrannical power.** The Declaration of Independence claims a right to overthrow a despotic ruler.
ex.tip: Words about power are worth sorting by how much is held and how it is checked.

opts: The heat made everyone indolent, and nothing got done all afternoon
She was so indolent that she finished three projects before noon
The indolent storm damaged several roofs
He gave an indolent and detailed account of the meeting
steps: Indolent means indulging in ease, avoiding exertion, lazy.
Heat making everyone indolent so nothing gets done matches exactly.
Finishing three projects contradicts it, and storms and accounts cannot be lazy.

ex.main: **The heat made everyone lazy.** Indolence is chosen ease, not exhaustion.
ex.tip: When an option contradicts the definition in the same sentence, it is usually the deliberate trap.

questions.q: A columnist writes: "I have grown cynical about campaign promises." She means she now:
opts: Believes them more readily than before
questions.hint: Cynicism is about motives, not comprehension.
steps: Cynical means doubtful of the sincerity of others' motives.
Growing cynical about promises means suspecting the people making them do not mean them.
It is a judgement about sincerity — not about clarity or legality.

ex.main: **She doubts the sincerity behind them.** Cynicism targets motive, which is why it is hard to argue someone out of.
ex.tip: Cynical and skeptical are close but not identical: skeptics doubt the claim, cynics doubt the person.

questions.q: A biologist says overfarming has "impoverished" the soil. She means the soil has:
opts: Been stripped of what made it rich
questions.hint: Impoverish has a sense beyond money.
steps: Impoverish means to make poor — and its second sense is simply to take away.
Applied to soil, it means the nutrients that made it fertile have been removed.
The word is about depletion, not money, poison or texture.

ex.main: **Stripped of what made it rich.** The money sense is the common one; the depletion sense is the one science uses.
ex.tip: When a familiar word appears in an unfamiliar field, look for its literal core — here, "made poor" becomes "depleted".

questions.q: Which use of contemporary matches the book’s NOUN definition?
opts: Mozart and Haydn were contemporaries who admired each other’s work
The gallery specialises in contemporary art from the last decade
She prefers contemporary furniture to antiques
The building has a contemporary glass façade
questions.hint: The noun means a person living at the same time as another.
steps: As a noun, a contemporary is a person living during the same period as another.
Mozart and Haydn living and working at the same time makes them contemporaries.
The other three use the adjective to mean modern — a real meaning, but not the noun asked for.

ex.main: **Mozart and Haydn were contemporaries.** The noun says nothing about being modern — two people in 1780 were contemporaries.
ex.tip: This is the single most common error with this word. "Contemporary" as a noun is about sharing a time with someone, not with us.

steps: Voracious means ravenously hungry — the first word is the extreme version of the second.
So the relationship is degree, running from ordinary up to intense.
Sagacious means deeply wise — the same jump beyond ordinary wisdom. Match.
Callow and experienced are opposites, a despot is a type of ruler, and wane and weaken are simply synonyms.

ex.main: **Both pairs are DEGREE: the first word is the intense form of the second.** Voracious is hunger turned up; sagacious is wisdom turned up.
ex.tip: Degree, synonym and type-to-category all look similar at a glance. The test is whether one word is STRONGER, the SAME, or a KIND OF the other.

questions.hint: Is every ruler a despot, or every despot a ruler?
steps: A despot is a specific KIND of ruler — one with absolute power.
So the relationship is: specific type to general category.
A cynic is a specific kind of skeptic — one who doubts motives. Match.
Venerate and despise are opposites, strife and conflict are synonyms, and wane is the opposite of grow.

ex.main: **Both pairs are TYPE TO CATEGORY.** Every despot is a ruler and every cynic is a skeptic, but not the reverse.
ex.tip: Use the one-way test: "every A is a B, but not every B is an A." If it only works one way, it is type-to-category.

questions.hint: What does a callow person not yet have?
steps: Callow means young and inexperienced — the adjective names what is MISSING.
So the pattern is: adjective : the quality it lacks.
Indolent means lacking energy — avoiding exertion. Match.
Secular means worldly (synonym), speculate means to guess (synonym), and an impediment IS an obstacle (synonym).

ex.main: **Both pairs are ADJECTIVE : WHAT IT LACKS.** The callow lack experience; the indolent lack energy.
ex.tip: Three of the four options here are plain synonyms. When most options share one relationship, the odd one out is often the answer.

questions.hint: Does venerating add respect or remove it?
steps: To venerate is to show GREAT respect — the verb intensifies and delivers the noun.
Look for a pair where the verb acts strongly ON the noun in the same direction.
To impoverish is to strip away wealth — the verb acts on the noun, but by removing it.
Weigh the options: enunciate and pronounce are synonyms, strife and peace are opposites, and callow simply means young.
Only impoverish shows a verb operating directly on the quantity of a noun, which is the closest structural match.

ex.main: **Both pairs are VERB ACTING ON A QUANTITY: venerate raises respect, impoverish lowers wealth.** The direction differs; the structure is what the analogy tests.
ex.tip: Not every analogy has a perfect answer — sometimes you pick the CLOSEST structure. Rule out the plain synonyms and opposites first.

questions.q: A historian writes that a leader "was venerated by his contemporaries but is viewed cynically today." What does this sentence claim?
opts: People of his own era revered him; later observers doubt his motives
He was disliked in his lifetime and admired afterwards
He was equally admired in both periods
His contemporaries never wrote about him
questions.hint: Sort out who is speaking in each half.
steps: Venerated means shown great respect; his contemporaries are the people living at the same time as him.
So the first half says the people of his own era revered him.
Cynically means doubting sincerity of motive, and "today" moves us to the present.
So reputations reversed: reverence then, suspicion now.

ex.main: **Revered in his own time, doubted now.** The whole sentence turns on knowing that contemporaries means people of HIS era, not ours.
ex.tip: Reputation-over-time sentences are common in history writing. Track WHO is judging in each clause before deciding what changed.

questions.q: Which two Lesson 5 words could describe the same person from opposite viewpoints?
opts: sagacious and cynical — one credits sound judgement, the other suspicion of motives
despot and tyrant — both mean the same thing
strife and conflict — both mean the same thing
wane and diminish — both mean the same thing
questions.hint: Only one of these pairs disagrees with itself.
steps: The question asks for words that describe one person from OPPOSING viewpoints.
A person who assumes others have bad motives can be called sagacious (they read people well) or cynical (they assume the worst).
The other three pairs are synonyms — they agree, so they cannot express opposite views.

ex.main: **Sagacious and cynical.** The same caution looks like wisdom to an ally and sourness to a critic.
ex.tip: Choosing between near-neighbours like these is how writers signal their sympathies while appearing to just describe.

questions.hint: Speech class is where you practise it.
steps: Enunciate means to pronounce clearly.
Learning to enunciate in speech class is about clarity, not volume.
Its second sense — to state or announce — is also about making something clear.

ex.main: **Pronounce clearly.** Enunciation is about crispness of sound, not loudness.
ex.tip: Clear and loud are different qualities. A whisper can be well enunciated.

questions.q: A financial page reports that an investor "speculated" in currency markets. This means she:
opts: Took a risky position hoping for profit
questions.hint: Speculate has an everyday sense and a financial one.
steps: Speculate means to think about or make guesses — and in business, to engage in a risky venture.
On a financial page, the business sense is the live one.
The book's own example is losing money speculating in the stock market.
So she took a risky position, not merely observed.

ex.main: **Took a risky position hoping for profit.** The financial sense keeps the guesswork of the everyday sense and adds money to it.
ex.tip: When a word appears in a specialist context, check whether that field has claimed a narrower sense of it.

questions.q: Which sentence uses secular in a way that contrasts it correctly with religion?
opts: The school teaches ethics from a secular perspective, without reference to any faith
The secular ceremony was held inside the cathedral by a bishop
She has a secular interest in ancient languages
The secular weather kept everyone indoors
questions.hint: Secular means worldly, not connected with religion.
steps: Secular means worldly; not connected with a church or religion.
Teaching ethics without reference to any faith is exactly a secular approach.
A ceremony run by a bishop in a cathedral is the opposite of secular, and interests and weather cannot be secular at all.

ex.main: **Ethics taught without reference to faith.** Secular is defined by the absence of religious grounding.
ex.tip: Secular pairs with temporal from Lesson 4 — both mean "of this world" and both are defined against the spiritual.
